title: Book 1 — Clio, Chapter 118
paragraphs: When Harpagos heard this, he made obeisance and thought it a great matter that his offense had turned out for his profit, and moreover that he had been invited to dinner with such a happy omen. So he went to his house. Having entered, he at once sent forth his son — for he had one only son, about thirteen years old — bidding him go to the palace of Astyages and do whatever the king commanded, and overjoyed he told his wife what had befallen him. But Astyages, when the son of Harpagos arrived, cut his throat and divided him limb from limb, and having roasted some pieces of the flesh and boiled others, he had them dressed for eating and kept them ready. When the time came for dinner and the other guests were present, including Harpagos, then before the other guests and before Astyages himself were placed tables covered with mutton; but before Harpagos was placed the flesh of his own son — all but the head, hands, and feet, which were laid aside, covered up, in a basket. When it seemed that Harpagos had had enough food, Astyages asked him whether he had been pleased with the banquet. When Harpagos said he had been very greatly pleased, those who had been commanded to do so brought to him the head of his son, covered up, together with the hands and the feet. Standing near, they bade Harpagos uncover and take whichever of them he desired. When Harpagos obeyed and uncovered them, he saw the remains of his son. Seeing them, he was not overcome with amazement but contained himself. Astyages asked him whether he knew of what animal he had been eating the flesh, and he said that he knew, and that whatever the king might do was well pleasing to him. Having made this reply and taking up the parts of the flesh that remained, he went to his house; and afterwards, I suppose, he would gather all the parts together and bury them.
